books.section: Unit 5: Toward the Civil War and Reconstruction (1844–1877)

stimulus.source_note: Immigration figures: U.S. Bureau of the Census, Historical Statistics of the United States. Rounded figures.
stimulus.text:
| Decade | Immigrants arriving in the United States |
| 1831–1840 | about 600,000 |
| 1841–1850 | about 1.7 million |
| 1851–1860 | about 2.6 million |

source: original; stimulus as noted in stimulus.source_note
stem: The table’s figures help explain the rise of nativism most directly because they show that

options.text: newcomers arrived fast enough to change Northern cities.

options.misconception: Background from the books: immigrants crowded into Northern port cities like New York and Boston; the cities are where nativism grew loudest.

options.text: the South received most of the new immigrants.
options.misconception: Background from the books: the newcomers settled mainly in the North, where factories and ports offered wage work; the South drew few immigrants.

options.text: immigration had no effect on American politics.
options.misconception: Background from the books: the Know-Nothing Party’s electoral wins in the 1850s show the opposite: immigration reshaped politics within a decade.

rationales.A: Background from the books: millions of newcomers in two decades remade the cities they settled in, and native-born Americans who felt crowded out organized against them.
rationales.B: Background from the books: immigrants crowded into Northern port cities like New York and Boston; the cities are where nativism grew loudest.
rationales.C: Background from the books: the newcomers settled mainly in the North, where factories and ports offered wage work; the South drew few immigrants.
rationales.D: Background from the books: the Know-Nothing Party’s electoral wins in the 1850s show the opposite: immigration reshaped politics within a decade.
rationales.general:
1. Feel the scale: about 4.3 million arrivals in twenty years, most landing in Northern ports.
2. Background from the books: those newcomers crowded into cities, keeping their languages and Catholic faith.
3. See the reaction: rapid change in a city feeds the fear that nativism turns into politics.
Remember: numbers explain a movement when they show how fast a place changed.
